nameStory: This little spider gets its scientific name from Pennsylvania, where early specimens were first collected and described by scientists. The name 'pennsylvanicum' literally means 'from Pennsylvania,' though this tiny cobweb weaver has since been found throughout much of eastern North America. It's a classic example of how a species can be named after the place where researchers happened to first study it, even though it lives in many other places too!
description: The Pennsylvania Cobweb Spider is a tiny member of the comb-footed spider family, builders of the classic sticky, tangled webs we often call cobwebs. These diminutive spiders are quite small, typically measuring just a few millimeters across including their legs. Like other cobweb spiders, they have rounded abdomens and relatively thin legs, with the classic 'comb' of bristles on their back legs that they use to throw silk over prey. Their webs are irregular, three-dimensional tangles rather than the neat orb webs of garden spiders.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small spider, with body length typically just 2-3 millimeters - about the size of a large pinhead or small peppercorn

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates irregular, three-dimensional cobwebs in corners and crevices that feel sticky and somewhat dusty when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, bulbous abdomen with thin legs; overall body feels delicate and would be easily crushed if handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in web center or retreats quickly to web edges when disturbed, moving with jerky, stop-and-go motions

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight tiny eyes arranged in two rows, though these are barely visible without magnification on such a small spider

habitat: Look for these tiny spiders in protected corners and crevices around buildings, under eaves, in basement corners, and among dense vegetation. They prefer sheltered spots where their small webs won't be destroyed by wind or rain. In natural settings, they're often found under rock overhangs, in hollow logs, or among the tangled stems of shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build webs in protected corners. Look for fresh, clean cobwebs appearing in previously web-free spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most noticeable and spiders are actively hunting. Egg sacs may be visible as small, papery spheres attached to web strands.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings increased activity, with males often found wandering in search of females. Webs may become more numerous in sheltered areas.
seasonality.winter: Many individuals overwinter as juveniles or young adults in protected locations, often becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being so tiny you could fit several on your thumbnail, these spiders are actually related to the infamous black widow - they're both comb-footed spiders that use the same silk-throwing technique to capture prey, just scaled way down!
confusionNotes: With only one confirmed observation in New England, this species is easily confused with its more common relatives like the Eastern Long-legged Cobweaver. The key is location and web structure - look for the characteristic irregular cobwebs rather than trying to distinguish the tiny spiders themselves without magnification.
contextualKnowledge: This species highlights how much we still don't know about small spiders - with only one recorded observation in New England, it may be either genuinely rare in the region or simply overlooked due to its tiny size. Many small cobweb spiders require expert identification to distinguish between species.
compareHints: This species is very similar to other Theridion spiders found in New England, particularly the Eastern Long-legged Cobweaver, but tends to be smaller and has slightly different web placement preferences. The White Long-legged Cobweaver is often lighter in coloration, while the Fence Long-legged Cobweaver typically builds webs on man-made structures. Without microscopic examination, these tiny relatives are nearly impossible to distinguish reliably in the field.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Theridion relatives in New England, the Eastern Long-legged Cobweaver is distinguished by its habitat preferences and web placement rather than dramatic visual differences.

Among its Theridion relatives, the White Long-legged Cobweaver stands out for its notably pale, whitish coloration compared to the darker Eastern Long-legged Cobweaver or the more boldly marked Fence Long-legged Cobweaver.

Among its Theridion relatives, the Fence Long-legged Cobweaver stands out for its strong association with human-made structures, while the Eastern Long-legged Cobweaver prefers natural vegetation and the White Long-legged Cobweaver is typically found on tree bark.
The Different Cobweb Spider is distinguished from its Theridion relatives primarily by subtle differences in body markings and proportions.
